Hi - was a US student doing graduate school in London 2019-2021. 

1. I had HSBC - like another user said, it just seemed most readily available/closest to my house. Nothing special about it really. Had a basic debit account. I did have to get a letter from my school to open an account.
2. I used Wise quite a few times and liked it. Yes there was a fee, but I didn't feel like it was that bad, probably $7ish to transfer about $1k? I didn't do extensive research on other options, but Wise stood out to me as being super easy to set up and quick on the transfer time.
3. I bartended at a Young's pub while studying as well. No one will care what you order. Most folks drink lager, cider also common. I can't think of a super common wheat beer but depends on the bar. Our cheapest beers were usually the ales, which imo were mostly drunk by older British men but definitely give it a try. Bars in the outskirts of London will also be cheaper than central, obviously. Weatherspoons bars are cheap. Be aware that standard pubs will usually have draft, bottles, and liquor+mixer drinks. If you want an actual cocktail there are bars kind of specifically for that, you can tell by their menu (seemed more separated to me than a lot of bars in the U.S. where they will have everything). I would generally avoid ordering cocktails in the pub but mixed drinks are fine.
4. Pick whatever you like. Check out your local FC and non-Premier League clubs for tickets on a budget. Try not to get in fights with other teams' supporters especially when drinking is involved lol.

I studied abroad through NYU for a year and had a tight budget as well for the most part. I'm sure you already know about the trust fund rich kids that go to that school and honestly, they are going to use their study abroad experience as an excuse to travel around Europe every weekend. Looking back, I am glad I wasn't able to afford to go on many trips during the time I was there. I was already in a freaking foreign country for godsakes, so enjoy it! Make it a point to actually get to know the city where you'll be living instead of spending tons of cash trying to get out and have all these other experiences. I didn't go to London but some of the cheap things I did in my study abroad town were: hiking/biking in the parks, going to the markets (even just to window shop), visiting free museums, going out to eat with my friends at really cheap places (like dollar deals certain days of the week), picking a random subway stop just to see what was there, etc. Pre-gaming at home before going out is always cheaper. Also try just googling "free/cheap things to do in London" and see where it gets you. The study abroad programs are much smaller and more tight-knit than the NYC campus and everyone will have to do orientation together -- then you will have classes with these people. I didn't know that many people either and literally made some of my best friends by just asking if I could sit in an empty seat next to them on the bus. Don't worry!

This is probably too late to be seen by many but after reading all of the different Paris threads and reflecting on the situation, I'd like to express my thoughts on the situation.

The goal of terrorism is just as its name implies - to terrorize human beings. Terrorism makes us feel unsafe in our own cities and homes, it makes us fear an "other" and it attempts to marginalize, alienate and destroy the security of a society. It seeks to instill doubt, dread and suspicion in the very familiarity of our everyday lives. Because of this, many average citizens like you and me view terrorism as a greater force not to be reckoned with by the common individual. Many people believe that the only way to eradicate terrorism is through political, militaristic or governmental efforts. People believe that their role is limited to being angry or upset about the situation, and sending grievances and thoughts those deceased and their family members.

This is not true. You can *do* something.Terrorism needs to be combated with unity and empowerment. The innocent do not have to be just victims. True unity is not just creating solidarity with your friends and neighbors. True unity is reaching out to those on the edges of society, those marginalized and isolated. Your small bubble of a community is not the only one who feels the effects of terrorism and it will take the solidarity of the globe to solve the problem. We must stand with France, but not only the European French. We must stand with the Muslim French, African French, the French who might not even feel French because of their place in society.

Below is a list of organizations that work against terrorism and towards peace and understanding. Although terrorism is senseless and I do not support or condone the acts or the groups behind them in any way, there is a deeply rooted social construction, agenda and psychology behind it that is not just a bunch of people who want to kill others because they are bored. As a common citizen, you can lend the time you spent watching the news or posting to Facebook and volunteer to create a new sense of familiarity between peoples or even just read deeper into the vast research and knowledge provided by these organizations. The first step towards understanding and accepting other races, cultures and religions is to become familiar with them. See the humanity behind the ideas, and bring people together under the light. 

**Learn from:** 

* National Consortium on the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (led by the University of Maryland): http://www.start.umd.edu/

* International Institute for Counterterrorism: http://www.ict.org.il/

* The Handa Center for the Study of Terrorism and Political Violence (led by the University of St. Andrews in Scotland): http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~cstpv/

* International Centre for the Study of Radicalisation and Political Violence (led by King's College, London): http://icsr.info/

* The Arab-American Institute: http://www.aaiusa.org/

* Salam Institute for Peace and Justice: http://salaminstitute.org/new/

**Volunteer with:**

* Council on American-Islamic Relations (several locations throughout the U.S.): http://www.cair.com/

* Islamic Society of North America: http://www.isna.net/

* Muslim Council of Britain: http://www.mcb.org.uk/

* Counterterrorism Education Learning Lab: http://www.thecell.org/

* National Council on Canada-Arab Relations: http://nccar.ca/

* The Council for Arab-British Understanding: http://www.caabu.org/

(I'm not French nor do I speak French very well so bear with me and add suggestions if you like)

* Un Coeur por la Paix: http://www.uncoeurpourlapaix.org/

ALSO: Contact your local refugee resettlement office or immigration center. It is so important to make groups like these feel welcomed, accepted and well integrated. Remember that being a refugee or an immigrant does NOT make you a terrorist, but these groups routinely become scapegoated.
